title: LoRA in Token Factory: multi-LoRA on dedicated endpoints
focus:
Audience: inference-infrastructure engineers on Nebius Token Factory. They already know LoRA math, merged vs unmerged serving, Punica, S-LoRA and vLLM/SGLang multi-LoRA (a previous episode), and the next-door episode covers Token Factory's architecture. Target length about 30 minutes, no more than 35: be dense and do not repeat points, no warm-up, no hype opening, no analogies longer than one sentence. Give every numbered item below real depth; a previous attempt rushed items 3, 5 and 10 into one-liners. At most one minute of LoRA refresher plus platform recap combined.

Cover, in this order:
1. Why LoRA is broken on dedicated endpoints today (UI hard-codes training type full, the public API hides kind lora, the DE API says "Only full custom weights are supported for dedicated endpoints", the data plane 404s dedicated/<key>:<adapter> because it registers only the routing key by exact match, serverless LoRA deploy returns 410 since July 2026) and the merge workaround with its costs.
2. Demand shapes with customer names. Shape A: Spiich, Parloa, Cresta. Shape B: Cursive (91.3 GiB, BF16, rank 64, on MXFP4 routed experts of a Kimi base, rotated 5 to 6 times a day). For Parloa state two separate facts and do not link them causally: pressure dropped on 18 August when it moved to R&D; separately, Gemma-4 LoRA was reported unsupported in vLLM and SGLang at the time. The deals linked to TOFA-51 total about $1.53M MRR and are exactly Parloa, Revolut, Fastino, Prosus and Prorata; do not add other names to that list. Prosus, Wix and Revolut separately list DE LoRA as a blocker.
3. The PRD (owned by the PM for dedicated endpoints, Konstantin Musatov): artifact, allow-list, addressing with the reserved colon, no fallback to base, rolling-update attach/detach. When explaining why v1 is rolling and not hot-swap, use only the sources' reasons: the scope is deliberately fenced, in-place load (C3) needs a security review, and vLLM marks runtime load as development-only. C1/C2/C3 with who each serves, and all four Stages 0 to 3 with who uses each stage and each stage's exit condition (including Stage 2's measured limits and docs, and Stage 3's naming, engine set, per-adapter observability and billing). The full out-of-scope list. No LoRA-specific pricing, with the approver's quote. The comment debate as the source states it: unbounded adapter sets, frequent zero-downtime changes, Fireworks' BF16-only multi-LoRA suggesting about 4x memory against a quantized fleet; do not explain a mechanism for the 4x figure, just attribute it; the reviewer conceded "the roster is very convincing"; the memory worry went into OQ-4; C1-only is the fallback.
4. OQ-1 to OQ-9: these are the PRD's open questions, with suggested positions from the research report. One or two sentences each, with owners.
5. Services and teams: walk service by service, naming the owning team and the concrete change for each: model-weights-api and worker (tf-endpoints), CPL (Business stream, tf-cpl), templates (tf-endpoints with the Models stream), endpoints-controller (tf-endpoints), the Helm chart (tf-orchestra, cryod parts tf-elastic), DPL (tf-dpl), billing (tf-billing-dev), router and engine-proxy (tf-orchestra), frontend (tokenfactory-fe), cryod (tf-elastic), post-training (tokenfactory-ft). 14 components are touched, 8 of them substantively. The PR plan is about 40 single-team merge requests; six can start immediately (including the billing fix, the router fix and the limits benchmark).
6. The six code traps and fixes. The billing trap is about per-token DEDICATED endpoints, not serverless; do not invent prices. Router trap: treat a model containing a colon as a LoRA request.
7. Engine knobs: flag names exactly; memory pre-allocated by the envelope (max_loras slots times max_lora_rank times LoRA-capable modules); runtime load behind VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING and its development-only warning. The old 15 to 25 percent overhead figure is from vLLM 0.6.3, stale, and must be re-measured. MoE math: the rank-64 BF16 expert adapter estimate is about 76 GiB, which matches Cursive's 91.3 GiB in order of magnitude; about 4 percent of the parameters but about 15 percent of the bytes of the MXFP4 base's routed experts.
8. Competitors: one short segment, two minutes at most. The differentiators (LoRA on quantized and MoE bases, per-adapter observability, large adapters with a documented budget, explicit errors for unknown adapters) are opportunities Token Factory could win with, not features it already ships.
9. The demo: real vLLM 0.12, Qwen3-1.7B, one H200, three trained adapters, five rejected broken adapters with their reasons, attach and detach about 54 seconds on real vLLM. Drain before stop: the first roll had exactly ONE HTTP 500 out of 440 requests; after the fix, load rounds of 1,733 and 1,769 requests had zero failures, run with the stub engine in place of vLLM. Then the six lessons, one or two sentences each with the concrete detail (e.g. vLLM 0.22 needs driver 580 or newer, 0.11 crashed on the playground's response_format, 0.12 worked; the ~10 second allow-list propagation lag).
10. The EDR draft, with depth: its TL;DR, the key positions (list-valued from day one, kind lora plus side table, allow-list table, statuses kept, rank capped at attach, delivery via S3 staging, bad adapter at engine start rolls back to the last good generation, cryod disabled for LoRA endpoints in v1 with the envelope hashed and the list not, security, no attach-latency SLO), each of iterations 0 to 3 with its constraint, the proposed (not yet agreed) limits benchmark with its four measurements, and the starred questions it still needs answered (driver and approvers, C1+C2 scope, entity shape, where rank is capped, delivery and cross-region replication, bad adapter at engine start, cryod in v1, who measures limits).

Rules: state only facts from the sources and attribute them (PRD, code reading, demo, EDR draft). Do not invent reasons, prices, failure scenarios or consequences that the sources don't state. Say flag names exactly; do not read file paths, URLs or regexes aloud. End with a concrete recap of the next decisions (D1 adapter list outside the hash, delivery, attachment model, alias spec, who runs the benchmark, cryod in v1). Do not end with a question or a "something to think about" thought.

# Episode 47 review log

## Take 1 (deep-dive, long, focus1.txt): 56:06, rejected
Coverage was complete (all OQs, six traps, flags, demo, EDR) and the stub-engine caveat for 1,733/1,769 was stated correctly. Problems:
- Length 56 min vs 25-30 target; hype opening ("thousands of dollars... 50 MB file on an H200", churn risk) and a speculative closing question about network saturation.
- Wrong: the $1.53M MRR list said "Prosus, Wix, Fastino, ProRata, Revolut" (source: Parloa, Revolut, Fastino, Prosus, Prorata).
- Wrong causality: Parloa's pressure dropped "because Gemma-4 LoRA was unsupported"; sources give these as two separate facts (moved to R&D on 18.08).
- Wrong attribution: OQ-1..9 called EDR questions the Elastic team had to answer; they are PRD open questions. The PRD itself was also described as authored by the Elastic team (owner is the PM, Musatov).
- Invented rationale for rolling updates (memory fragmentation, state corruption) instead of the PRD's (fenced scope, security review, vLLM's dev-only runtime load).
- Lesson 1 said "massive spikes of HTTP 500 errors"; the source has one 500 out of 440 requests.
- MoE math: said overhead and KV cache "perfectly validate" the 91.3 GiB; the source says the 76 GiB estimate matches it in order of magnitude.
- "14 components owned by eight teams" (source: 14 components, 8 substantively touched); "work must flow strictly sequentially" (six PRs can start now).
- Billing trap framed as a "shared per-token tier" with an invented "two cents a token"; source: per-token dedicated endpoints.
- Minor invented details: crash loop on delete, DDoS of the controller, "OOM instantly at max-loras 20", "the EDR mandates the benchmark" (it is proposed, Q-L1), "without an approver the 40 PRs can't merge".
Prompt change for take 2: length default; strict word-for-word lists for the MRR accounts and Parloa; attribute OQs to the PRD; give the PRD's rolling-update rationale; the 1-in-440 figure; the order-of-magnitude MoE wording; forbid invented prices, rationales and closing questions; cap intro at 1 min with no hype.

## Take 2 (deep-dive, default, focus2.txt): 15:22, rejected
Fixed every take-1 accuracy issue (MRR list, Parloa as two facts, OQs attributed to the PRD, the PRD's three reasons for rolling updates, one 500 in 440, MoE "order of magnitude", stub-engine caveat, concrete recap ending). Problems:
- Too short (15 min vs 25-30): service-by-service team ownership, Stage 2/3 exit conditions, EDR iterations and the EDR's open questions were reduced to one-liners.
- Invented explanation of the debate's "4x memory" (BF16 adapters exploding against a quantized base); the source says Fireworks' BF16-only multi-LoRA hints at about 4x memory against our quantized fleet, without further mechanism.
- Overclaim: listed per-adapter observability, large-adapter budgets etc. as things Token Factory "has"; the report lists them as differentiators it could win with.
Prompt change for take 3: length long, with explicit about-30-minute pacing and per-section depth requirements (team per service, all four stage exits, each EDR iteration, the starred EDR questions); keep take-2 constraints; differentiators framed as opportunities; no mechanism for the 4x claim.

## Take 3 (deep-dive, long, focus3.txt): 20:32, published
Checked against the source files: capability and stage definitions with exit conditions, OQ-1..9 owners and positions, team per service, the six traps and fixes, flag names and the runtime-load env var with its warning, the stale 15-25% (vLLM 0.6.3), MoE 76 GiB vs 91.3 GiB order of magnitude and 4%/15%, demo numbers (54 s on real vLLM; one 500 in 440; 0 failures in 1,733 and 1,769 on the stub engine), MRR list and Parloa facts, competitors as opportunities, concrete ending. No credentials, IPs or hosts.
Minor imprecisions left: OQ-7 omits the original Q3 promise; OQ-3 says reserve the colon "for future addressing" (source: a future colon for versions); "existing statuses are capped" (kept); router trap called "massive collisions". Shorter than the 25-30 min target, and the 42 MB-91.3 GiB size range is not stated. Take limit (3) reached; accuracy judged good enough to publish.
